introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 3 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: 1 hour 45 minutes.**

INSTRUCTIONS TO CANDIDATES: Answer ANY THREE questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are advised to spend the first fifteen minutes reading the paper. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
This question is based on the passage below:

> "In all societies people want more than they are capable of producing. At any given moment in time the supply of economic resources is limited, so that more of one thing can be produced only if less of something else is produced. Likewise, incomes are limited and in spending our incomes we have to choose between alternatives. Economists use the term **"opportunity cost"** to describe the idea of measuring cost in terms of the alternatives forgone. This is a very important concept. We have to make choices all the time. We have to decide how we spend our time, how we spend our incomes and what employment we undertake...
>
> Producers and governments also have to make choices. A producer must decide what goods to produce and which resources to employ. For example, a farmer opting to use an area of land for growing corn has chosen not to use it for another purpose e.g. keeping sheep. In growing the corn, he has the choice of using **labour intensive or capital-intensive methods**. Governments also have to consider the opportunity cost of any decision they make. The real cost of building a hospital is not the cost in terms of money but cost in terms of the alternative uses of the resources i.e. the opportunity cost".

*Source: Adapted from Stanlake's Introductory Economics, 7th Edition. Page 9.*

questions.enonce_markdown:
Define:

(i) economic resources. (2 marks)

(ii) opportunity cost. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Economic resources** (also called **factors of production**) are the **scarce inputs that are used to produce goods and services**. They are classified as **land** (all natural resources), **labour** (human effort, physical and mental), **capital** (man-made aids to production such as machines, tools and buildings) and **enterprise** (the organisation of the other factors and the risk-taking). They are scarce because they are limited in supply relative to the many uses to which they can be put.

**(ii) Opportunity cost** is **the value of the next best alternative that is given up (forgone) when a choice is made**. For example, if a farmer uses a plot of land to grow maize, the opportunity cost is the income he would have earned from the best alternative use of that plot, such as keeping sheep.

questions.enonce_markdown: How is opportunity cost related to choice? (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Opportunity cost and choice are two sides of the same problem, which is **scarcity**.

- Resources and incomes are limited while human wants are unlimited, so **a choice has to be made** between competing uses.
- Because resources are scarce, **choosing one alternative means giving up another**. What is given up is the opportunity cost of the choice taken.
- Therefore **every choice has an opportunity cost, and opportunity cost measures the real cost of a choice**: the greater the value of the alternative forgone, the more costly the decision. Rational consumers, producers and governments compare the benefit of the option chosen with its opportunity cost before deciding.

For example, a household that spends its income on a television chooses not to buy the food or school fees it could have bought instead: that forgone alternative is the opportunity cost.

questions.enonce_markdown: Why is opportunity cost considered more important than cost measured in monetary terms? (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Cost measured in money (the **money or accounting cost**) records only the cash that is paid out. Opportunity cost is considered more important because:

1. **It measures the real sacrifice of resources.** Money cost does not show what the resources could have produced elsewhere, whereas opportunity cost measures the benefits forgone. The real cost of a hospital is the schools, roads or water supplies that the same labour, materials and land could have provided.
2. **It includes costs that involve no payment.** The time of an owner-farmer, the use of land already owned, leisure given up or unpaid family labour have an opportunity cost although no money is spent.
3. **It helps in decision-making.** It forces a decision-maker to compare alternatives, so resources are allocated to their best use. Money prices can be distorted by taxes, subsidies, monopoly power or inflation and may therefore not reflect the true scarcity of resources.

Hence two projects with the same money cost can have very different opportunity costs, and the one with the lower opportunity cost is the better choice.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Give two examples of the possible opportunity cost of government building a new hospital. (2 marks)

(ii) What is another name for opportunity cost? (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The opportunity cost of the hospital is the best alternative use of the same resources (any two, 1 mark each): **building a school** or a university; **building or tarring roads and bridges**; **providing safe drinking water and electricity** to villages; **a reduction in taxes** or a lower national debt; **spending on agriculture or housing** instead; the **alternative use of the land** on which the hospital stands.

**(ii)** Another name for opportunity cost is **real cost** (the term used by the passage), also called **alternative cost** or **forgone alternative** (the next best alternative given up).

questions.enonce_markdown: Why do consumers, producers and governments have to make choices? (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
They have to make choices because of **scarcity**: **resources are limited while wants are unlimited**, and each resource has more than one possible use.

- **Consumers** have limited incomes, so they must choose which goods and services to buy and how to divide their income between spending and saving.
- **Producers** have limited factors of production (land, labour, capital, enterprise) and limited finance, so they must decide what to produce, how to produce it and in what quantities.
- **Governments** have limited revenue from taxes and borrowing, so they must choose between competing needs such as health, education, defence and roads.

Since not everything can be had, to choose one thing is to give up another.

questions.enonce_markdown: Distinguish between labour intensive and capital-intensive methods of production mentioned in the passage. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The two methods differ in the **proportion in which labour and capital are combined**.

| | Labour-intensive method | Capital-intensive method |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Uses **a large amount of labour relative to capital** to produce output | Uses **a large amount of capital (machinery, equipment) relative to labour** |
| Example (growing corn) | Planting and harvesting by hand with hoes and machetes, many workers | Using tractors, ploughs and combine harvesters, few workers |
| Cost structure | Labour cost is the larger part of total cost | Capital cost (depreciation, interest) is the larger part of total cost |
| Typical use | Where labour is plentiful and cheap, capital scarce (many developing countries); services such as teaching | Where capital is plentiful relative to labour, large scale of output (mining, oil refining, mechanised farming) |

A farmer chooses the method by comparing the relative prices and productivity of labour and capital, which again involves opportunity cost.
